name: Arc
executive_summary: Arc launched its public mainnet on September 16, 2026, built by Circle as an institutional layer-1 running on Malachite, a Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus engine originally built for Tendermint and CometBFT. It's an EVM-compatible chain that runs entirely on USDC as its gas token, secured by permissioned validator institutions including BlackRock, DTCC, Visa, and Mastercard. First scored September 17, 2026 at one to two days old, the chain was reassessed at one month on October 18, 2026. Two categories moved: Real-World Utility rose from 32 to 36 and KYA from 28 to 34, lifting the TradFi score from 38 to 39 and the AI score from 44 to 45, with both tiers unchanged. TradFi Approved holds at 74 on the validator roster, while On-Chain Health stays at 13 and Tokenomics & Supply at 20, since the ARC token is still minted but not tradeable, staked, or governing anything, and on-chain research shows much of the early activity is concentrated in a few wallets. A November 2026 review changed no score: stablecoins on the chain grew to about $1.7 billion, but usage remains concentrated, the ARC token is still unlaunched, and the core protocol is still unaudited. The result is an extraordinary institutional foundation with a still-thin, partly non-organic usage record, and no independent audit of the core protocol yet.

key_findings: TradFi Approved scores 74, one of Arc's clearest strengths: the validators securing this chain are institutions like BlackRock, DTCC, Visa, Mastercard, ICE, and Standard Chartered, not partners or sponsors but the literal infrastructure of the network, confirmed by an independent on-chain read rather than a press release. The score sits below what that roster alone might suggest because the chain's operating record is about ten weeks long, and this framework weights a track record built over years more heavily than one built over weeks.

On-Chain Health scores 13. Stablecoins on Arc grew to about $1.7 billion by late November 2026 and DeFi deposits to about $590 million, but the activity behind them is narrow. Independent on-chain research found about 73% of the chain's USDC held by four addresses in late October, and real daily users down about 96% from the launch-day peak to roughly 13,000 by mid-November, with a few large wallets dominating trading volume. About 8,700 addresses are active on a typical day. That is not yet the broad, organic usage this category rewards.

Real-World Utility scores 36. Two Janus Henderson funds (JAAA and JTRSY) and a New York Life high-yield bond product (HYB) went live on Arc through Centrifuge on October 2, 2026, alongside Circle's own tokenized money-market fund, and Circle's StableFX currency-exchange service has run on Arc since late September 2026. These are deployed, but each fund is restricted to eligible non-U.S. institutional investors with high minimums, no Arc-specific fund holdings or StableFX volume have been published, and one major tracker (RWA.xyz) shows no distributed real-world-asset value on Arc as of November 2026. BlackRock's BUIDL is still not confirmed as deployed on this chain.

Tokenomics & Supply scores 20. Ten billion ARC tokens were minted at genesis with a disclosed 60/25/15 allocation, but the token is not tradeable, not staked, not used for gas, and does not govern anything. Circle's own materials describe the genesis mint as "not a commitment to publicly launch." The chain's actual transactional currency is USDC, Circle's own stablecoin, which carries no economic exposure to whether this network succeeds or fails.

Decentralization scores 47. The validator set read at 15 active validators at first scoring, with the largest holding 7.69% of voting power, a reasonably even split for a set this size, but only 5 of the 15 are needed to halt the network and only 9 to break its safety threshold. No change to the validator cohort has been reported since launch.

Security & Future-Proofing scores 22. Arc runs an active bug bounty that found and fixed a real consensus-layer vulnerability before mainnet launched, with no post-launch critical protocol disclosure found. But no independent audit of the chain's core protocol or its Malachite consensus layer has been published, and the consensus software's own repository still describes it as alpha and not externally audited. About ten weeks of operation without a reported halt, reorg or consensus incident is useful context, but it is a short record rather than a track record.

Regulatory & Risk scores 68. No enforcement action and no adverse classification exist against this chain or its token, compliance tooling from established providers is built in, and the operating company itself holds a federal trust charter and is separately publicly listed. The only distribution of the ARC token to date was a closed institutional presale to accredited investors, a minor note at this category's weight rather than a material risk.

Execution Layer scores 62. Transactions finalize in under a second with no reported congestion, and deterministic finality means the chain has no fork-choice reorgs by design. Fees are priced in USD-pegged USDC rather than a volatile native token, which matters for automated systems that need predictable costs. The open question is real load: day-one throughput was roughly 90 transactions per second against a stated design target above 3,000, so performance well beyond that remains untested.

Composability & Atomicity scores 68. Standard batching and permit tools (Multicall3, Permit2, a CREATE2 factory) are confirmed live at their expected addresses, and the chain shipped its own precompiles that let a batched call preserve the original caller's identity, solving an attribution problem most general-purpose EVM chains leave unsolved. The one gap: a smart-account factory address is still not listed in the chain's own official documentation, even though custody providers claim support.

Security Posture scores 15. No independent audit of the core protocol exists, and an outside technical review flagged that both the execution client and the consensus client run as a single implementation each, a double point of failure. Layered on top is validator concentration (15 validators at first scoring, the largest holding 7.69%) and an operating record of about ten weeks. An active bug bounty that already caught one real vulnerability before launch, and about ten weeks with no reported halt or consensus incident, are the things working in this category's favor.

Economic Predictability scores 35. Gas priced in USD-pegged USDC is a genuine plus for an automated system that can't tolerate volatile costs. Working against it: block production is entirely permissioned, and the chain has a live, enforced protocol-level mechanism that can block specific addresses from moving USDC, with no published commitment from any validator not to use it. No documented production use of that mechanism against an external address has been found.

Agent Tooling scores 45. Real, chain-specific infrastructure for autonomous agents exists rather than borrowed generic EVM tooling: agent wallets with policy limits, a small-payments mechanism, an agent marketplace, and a payment-facilitator service. Measured agent payments remain tiny: public trackers attribute only a few hundred x402 agent-payment settlements to Arc as of late November 2026, and the agent-commerce standard Arc helped develop (ERC-8183) is deployed only on testnet in Arc's own reference list.

Standards & Interoperability scores 58. Account abstraction is more than a compatibility claim here: the chain operator's own production wallet is built as a smart-contract account with real operational monitoring, and a native token-bridging mechanism avoids the custody risk of a typical lock-and-mint bridge. Held back because the canonical account-abstraction entry-point address is still not published anywhere official.

KYA scores 34. All three ERC-8004 agent registries (Identity, Reputation, and Validation) are deployed on mainnet. Registrations climbed to roughly 490,000 by late November 2026, but they are not matched by activity: only six validations have been recorded and only a few hundred agent payments have settled, and public airdrop guides have encouraged registering agents to accumulate points. The score credits a live identity pathway, not the registration count.

watch_items: The ARC token is the single biggest swing factor. It remains unlaunched (Circle's whitepaper page states 'ARC is not launched'): no trading, staking, governance or fee burn, with a move to proof-of-stake described for 2027. Any of those becoming live would be a direct re-credit candidate for Tokenomics & Supply.

No independent audit of the core protocol or the Malachite consensus software has been published. A published, scoped audit covering the running code would be a direct re-credit candidate on the security check and on both axes' security categories.

Real-world assets: the Centrifuge funds (JAAA, JTRSY, HYB) are deployed but no Arc-specific holdings are published, RWA.xyz shows no distributed asset value on Arc, and BlackRock's BUIDL is not confirmed on this chain. Published holdings, or BUIDL deploying, would be a re-credit candidate; evidence the deployed funds hold nothing would be a re-debit candidate.
StableFX, Circle's currency-exchange service, has been live on Arc since late September 2026 with no published volume. Measurable volume would be a Real-World Utility re-credit candidate.

Usage concentration: stablecoin balances and trading are concentrated in a few wallets, and real daily users fell sharply after launch. Broader, more organic distribution of activity would be a re-credit candidate for On-Chain Health.

Agent identity: about 490,000 ERC-8004 registrations against six validations and a few hundred agent payments. Real validation activity or material agent-driven payment volume would be a re-credit candidate for KYA and Agent Tooling.

Validators: Circle does not publish a live validator list or voting-power breakdown; readings range from about 12 to 15 active validators. A published breakdown, or the planned proof-of-stake move, would bear on Decentralization.

A live, enforced protocol-level mechanism can block specific addresses from moving USDC. Any documented production use against an external address would be a further consideration. Arc's opt-in privacy remains on the roadmap; going live with real use would be a Privacy re-credit candidate.

tiles.cheapest_tx_cost_note: Native USDC transfer (21,000 gas) at the 20 gwei protocol minimum base fee, paid in USDC; Arc targets about $0.001 for a standard token transfer.
tiles.fee_yield_note: Not measurable. This metric divides fee revenue by market cap, and the ARC token has no live market or market cap to divide by -- the chain's actual gas token, USDC, is not an investable asset this metric is designed to measure.
